For the correct-class probability $p_t$, focal loss is $-\alpha_t(1-p_t)^\gamma\log p_t$. When $p_t$ is near one, the modulation term sharply reduces an easy example's contribution; for a hard example it stays substantial. With $\gamma=2$, an easy example with $p_t=0.99$ receives a modulation factor of $10^{-4}$. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.02002)

This prevents huge numbers of easy background anchors from overwhelming the informative gradients in dense single-stage detection. Alpha handles class balancing, while gamma controls focusing; setting gamma to zero recovers weighted cross entropy. The modulation factor also participates in differentiation, so it is not simply a detached sample weight. Tune on detection metrics and calibration, since excessive focusing can overemphasize mislabeled or ambiguous examples. Architecture and optimization also contributed to RetinaNet's results.
